title: Stress, Burnout & Psychological Demands
description: Start with two introductory modules on the essential ideas and how to reason from evidence. Then practise applying the ideas in a detailed case.

glossary.definition: A response to demands that feel larger than the resources available at that moment.
glossary.example: A support worker feels tense ahead of a difficult week of appointments.
glossary.limit: Stress can rise during one week without becoming a persistent occupational pattern.

glossary.definition: What work requires from someone in time, attention or responsibility.
glossary.example: An employee is assigned extra cases while the team remains short-staffed.
glossary.limit: Demand is partly shaped by how much control and support a person has.

glossary.definition: Time and conditions that allow the effects of effort to settle.
glossary.example: After a demanding shift, someone has uninterrupted time away from work.
glossary.limit: Rest becomes less effective when work messages and unfinished tasks repeatedly intrude.

glossary.example: An employee feels depleted for months while the job's demands keep increasing.

nodes.title: Start here
nodes.body:
An exhausting week is not automatically burnout. To understand what is happening, we need to look at how long the demands have continued and how much influence someone has over them.

When is work tiring, and when have the conditions of working become a sustained problem?
nodes.sources: WHO ICD-11 occupational burnout; Bakker & Demerouti (2007), Job Demands–Resources model.

nodes.title: What stress means
nodes.body:
A response to demands that feel larger than the resources available at that moment.

For example: A support worker feels tense ahead of a difficult week of appointments.

One important limit: Stress can rise during one week without becoming a persistent occupational pattern.
nodes.sources: WHO ICD-11 occupational burnout; Bakker & Demerouti (2007), Job Demands–Resources model.

nodes.title: Find the first concept
nodes.prompt: Consider this example: A support worker feels tense ahead of a difficult week of appointments. Which concept is most directly demonstrated, without claiming anything beyond the example?
nodes.explanation: The example most directly supports stress. A response to demands that feel larger than the resources available at that moment. Stress can rise during one week without becoming a persistent occupational pattern.
nodes.counterexample: Burnout is an occupational phenomenon, not a diagnosis established by tiredness alone. Individual coping cannot compensate indefinitely for unmanageable demands.
nodes.sources: WHO ICD-11 occupational burnout; Bakker & Demerouti (2007), Job Demands–Resources model.

nodes.title: What recovery means
nodes.body:
Time and conditions that allow the effects of effort to settle.

For example: After a demanding shift, someone has uninterrupted time away from work.

One important limit: Rest becomes less effective when work messages and unfinished tasks repeatedly intrude.
nodes.sources: WHO ICD-11 occupational burnout; Bakker & Demerouti (2007), Job Demands–Resources model.

nodes.title: What burnout means
nodes.body:
A work-related pattern of exhaustion and growing distance from work, sometimes accompanied by reduced efficacy, associated with chronic occupational stress.

For example: An employee feels depleted for months while the job's demands keep increasing.

One important limit: Burnout is not diagnosed from one tired morning and does not replace assessment of other causes of fatigue.
nodes.sources: WHO ICD-11 occupational burnout; Bakker & Demerouti (2007), Job Demands–Resources model.

lessons.title: First notice what happened
lessons.teach: Read what is said before deciding why anyone said it.
lessons.objective: Apply foundations to observable evidence, uncertainty and proportional decisions.

nodes.title: A situation, not a diagnosis
nodes.body:
Priya runs a busy support service. Sam is a colleague who has noticed Priya working late for weeks.

You can describe an event accurately while remaining uncertain about why it happened.
nodes.sources: WHO ICD-11 occupational burnout; Bakker & Demerouti (2007), Job Demands–Resources model.

nodes.title: Listen before you interpret
nodes.prompt: Follow the four messages. Keep the difference between the words said and their possible meaning in mind.
nodes.explanation: The purpose is to connect the term to what can actually be observed.
nodes.counterexample: Burnout is an occupational phenomenon, not a diagnosis established by tiredness alone. Individual coping cannot compensate indefinitely for unmanageable demands.
nodes.sources: WHO ICD-11 occupational burnout; Bakker & Demerouti (2007), Job Demands–Resources model.
nodes.scenario: Priya runs a busy support service. Sam is a colleague who has noticed Priya working late for weeks.

turns.speaker: a
turns.text: I used to recover after a busy week. Lately I wake up tired before work even starts.

turns.speaker: b
turns.text: We've had an unusually demanding month. Is there any sign the workload is easing?

turns.speaker: a
turns.text: They added another caseload yesterday, and the vacant post still hasn't been filled.

turns.speaker: b
turns.text: Have you had any say in how much you're expected to manage?

checks.prompt: What is the most careful conclusion we can draw from the exchange so far?

options.label: We can describe what each speaker requested, while treating any account of their motives as provisional.
options.feedback: This keeps the distinction between what was said and why it may have been said. The latter requires more evidence.

options.label: We can take the last speaker’s explanation as the main cause, because it is the latest information.
options.feedback: Order of speaking does not determine evidential quality; the earlier words still matter.

options.label: We can give the two speakers’ interpretations equal weight, regardless of which one fits the details.
options.feedback: Plausible alternatives can receive different weights when the observed details support them differently.

options.label: We can infer that one speaker has a stable psychological trait if their response appears defensive.
options.feedback: A single interaction may reflect a situation rather than a trait that persists across settings.

options.label: We can stop analysing the situation because multiple explanations remain logically possible.
options.feedback: Uncertainty is a reason to test explanations, not to abandon reasoning.

checks.explanation: People can be sincere about their experience and still have incomplete explanations of why events happened. Burnout is an occupational phenomenon, not a diagnosis established by tiredness alone. Individual coping cannot compensate indefinitely for unmanageable demands.
checks.counterexample: Burnout is an occupational phenomenon, not a diagnosis established by tiredness alone. Individual coping cannot compensate indefinitely for unmanageable demands.

nodes.title: A description or an assumption?
nodes.prompt: Does the sentence report something we can check, or interpret what it might mean?
nodes.explanation: The spoken words are evidence about what was said. A theory of why somebody said them is an interpretation that may need testing.
nodes.counterexample: Burnout is an occupational phenomenon, not a diagnosis established by tiredness alone. Individual coping cannot compensate indefinitely for unmanageable demands.
nodes.sources: WHO ICD-11 occupational burnout; Bakker & Demerouti (2007), Job Demands–Resources model.

items.label: “I used to recover after a busy week. Lately I wake up tired before work even starts.”
Persistent demands exceed Priya's available time and influence. Recovery becomes difficult because the conditions that created the overload remain in place.
“We've had an unusually demanding month. Is there any sign the workload is easing?”
A short period of exceptional work can cause fatigue without a broader pattern of occupational burnout; sleep or health factors may also contribute.

nodes.title: Why the distinction matters
nodes.body:
A short period of exceptional work can cause fatigue without a broader pattern of occupational burnout; sleep or health factors may also contribute.

Burnout is an occupational phenomenon, not a diagnosis established by tiredness alone. Individual coping cannot compensate indefinitely for unmanageable demands.
nodes.sources: WHO ICD-11 occupational burnout; Bakker & Demerouti (2007), Job Demands–Resources model.

lessons.title: Two explanations can sound reasonable
lessons.teach: Evidence should be able to change which explanation you prefer.
lessons.objective: Apply foundations to observable evidence, uncertainty and proportional decisions.

nodes.title: Start with competing accounts
nodes.body:
Persistent demands exceed Priya's available time and influence. Recovery becomes difficult because the conditions that created the overload remain in place.

Another possibility: A short period of exceptional work can cause fatigue without a broader pattern of occupational burnout; sleep or health factors may also contribute.
nodes.sources: WHO ICD-11 occupational burnout; Bakker & Demerouti (2007), Job Demands–Resources model.

nodes.title: What should we find out?
nodes.prompt: Both interpretations are plausible. What would actually help choose between them?
nodes.explanation: Compare demands, control and resources over time, including what happens when tasks are formally reprioritised. The question is what would change our view, rather than what would merely confirm it.
nodes.counterexample: Burnout is an occupational phenomenon, not a diagnosis established by tiredness alone. Individual coping cannot compensate indefinitely for unmanageable demands.
nodes.sources: WHO ICD-11 occupational burnout; Bakker & Demerouti (2007), Job Demands–Resources model.

options.label: Ask the speakers how intense their feelings were and use the stronger reaction to identify the main cause.
options.feedback: The strength of a feeling does not establish its cause.

options.label: Ask for a longer account from the speaker who was most upset, since they experienced the largest impact.
options.feedback: The account matters, but the amount of distress is not a direct test of someone else’s motive.

options.label: Compare demands, control and resources over time, including what happens when tasks are formally reprioritised.
options.feedback: This observation could make a meaningful difference between the competing explanations.

options.label: Find a second argument and see whether it sounds similar without comparing what changed.
options.feedback: A similar argument can occur for different reasons; comparison requires the relevant circumstances.

options.label: Ask an uninvolved friend to guess which personality type best describes the speaker.
options.feedback: A personality guess is less useful than identifying a testable difference between the proposed processes.

nodes.title: Something new has been found
nodes.body: A workload review shows Priya's caseload has risen by 40% while staffing has fallen, and the service has rejected every request to prioritise tasks.
nodes.sources: WHO ICD-11 occupational burnout; Bakker & Demerouti (2007), Job Demands–Resources model.

nodes.title: Revise your view
nodes.prompt: Which response to this new information is justified?
nodes.explanation: Documented organisational demands strongly support a structural explanation. A plan focused only on Priya's resilience would neglect the maintaining conditions.
nodes.counterexample: Burnout is an occupational phenomenon, not a diagnosis established by tiredness alone. Individual coping cannot compensate indefinitely for unmanageable demands.
nodes.sources: WHO ICD-11 occupational burnout; Bakker & Demerouti (2007), Job Demands–Resources model.

options.label: Keep the original explanation because it initially fitted the facts.
options.feedback: A reasonable earlier account can be revised as new evidence appears.

options.label: Prefer the explanation that most closely matches the new detail, while keeping other plausible causes open.
options.feedback: This revises confidence in response to information rather than to the apparent sophistication of the theory.

options.label: Treat the new evidence as decisive proof of a single hidden intention.
options.feedback: The evidence can favour an account without establishing complete access to another person’s motives.

options.label: Give every explanation identical weight because certainty is impossible.
options.feedback: Uncertainty does not require all accounts to be equally likely.

options.label: Ignore the new detail until each speaker independently agrees on its meaning.
options.feedback: Agreement may help cooperation, but it is not a prerequisite for evaluating evidence.

lessons.title: Ready for a real case
lessons.teach: You have the concepts. Now practise using them without jumping beyond the evidence.
lessons.objective: Apply foundations to observable evidence, uncertainty and proportional decisions.

lessons.title: When rest doesn't fix the workload
lessons.teach: Follow the conversation one message at a time. Notice what the behaviour might be achieving before you decide why it happened. About five minutes.
lessons.objective: Distinguish observable evidence from a tentative explanation of a busy week versus chronic overload.

nodes.title: Watch the conversation
nodes.prompt: Read the exchange one message at a time, then work from what the characters actually said.
nodes.sources: WHO, Burn-out: an occupational phenomenon; Bakker & Demerouti (2007), Job Demands-Resources model.
nodes.scenario: Priya works in a clinic where the number of appointments has increased without more staff.

turns.speaker: a
turns.text: I worked through lunch again and still missed two deadlines.

turns.speaker: b
turns.text: Did your workload change after the last review?

turns.speaker: a
turns.text: They added another clinic session. Nobody's hours increased.

turns.speaker: b
turns.text: Have you been able to recover outside work?

turns.speaker: a
turns.text: A weekend helps, but the backlog is larger every Monday.

turns.speaker: b
turns.text: What happens when you show management the number of hours available?

checks.prompt: Which psychological interpretation is currently best supported?

options.label: This may have been an exceptional week rather than a sustained demand problem.
The demands may exceed Priya's available time and support; personal organisation alone cannot close that gap.
Priya may need a more reliable way to prioritise urgent work.
The reaction may reflect an earlier expectation that neither speaker has described clearly in the exchange.
options.feedback: This is a reasonable line of inquiry, although The demands may exceed Priya's available time and support; personal organisation alone cannot close that gap. is more directly tied to the words in this scene. Fatigue can reflect other health or life factors. A full account needs the duration of demands and how work is affecting functioning.

options.label: The meaning of the event may differ between the speakers, even when they agree about the observable facts.
options.feedback: Different interpretations may contribute, but this is not yet specific enough to explain the response.

checks.explanation: The strongest clues are the character's own words. The demands may exceed Priya's available time and support; personal organisation alone cannot close that gap. Priya may need a more reliable way to prioritise urgent work. remains a legitimate rival, so this is a working account rather than a conclusion about personality.
checks.counterexample: Fatigue can reflect other health or life factors. A full account needs the duration of demands and how work is affecting functioning.

checks.prompt: You are Priya. Which response best addresses the practical problem at this point?

lessons.title: Choose a workable response
lessons.teach: Choose a response that serves a practical aim even when the other person does not cooperate.

nodes.title: Your influence has limits
nodes.body:
Burnout is an occupational phenomenon, not a diagnosis established by tiredness alone. Individual coping cannot compensate indefinitely for unmanageable demands.

An intervention can be reasonable even when the other person refuses it.

nodes.explanation: The first response is a proportionate attempt to address the problem directly. Escalation may be legitimate if that attempt fails. lessons.title: Try it in another situation
lessons.teach: Apply the way of reasoning to a different situation. Do not import the first case’s verdict.

nodes.title: A new situation
nodes.body:
A nurse takes repeated wellbeing workshops while staffing shortages and unsafe workload expectations remain unchanged.

Decide what you can infer from this example without assuming the same explanation must apply.

nodes.title: An idea worth carrying forward
nodes.body:
Persistent demands exceed Priya's available time and influence. Recovery becomes difficult because the conditions that created the overload remain in place.

Burnout is an occupational phenomenon, not a diagnosis established by tiredness alone. Individual coping cannot compensate indefinitely for unmanageable demands.

The purpose of the exercise is to make a better-supported judgement and choose a proportionate next step.

glossary.definition: A response to demands that feel larger than the resources available at that moment.
glossary.example: A support worker feels tense ahead of a difficult week of appointments.
glossary.limit: Stress can rise during one week without becoming a persistent occupational pattern.

glossary.definition: What work requires from someone in time, attention or responsibility.
glossary.example: An employee is assigned extra cases while the team remains short-staffed.
glossary.limit: Demand is partly shaped by how much control and support a person has.

glossary.definition: Time and conditions that allow the effects of effort to settle.
glossary.example: After a demanding shift, someone has uninterrupted time away from work.
glossary.limit: Rest becomes less effective when work messages and unfinished tasks repeatedly intrude.

glossary.definition: A work-related pattern of exhaustion and growing distance from work, sometimes accompanied by reduced efficacy, associated with chronic occupational stress.
glossary.example: An employee feels depleted for months while the job's demands keep increasing.
glossary.limit: Burnout is not diagnosed from one tired morning and does not replace assessment of other causes of fatigue.
